title: Mushtaq H. Khan (SOAS) — rents, rent-seeking and economic development framework
what_was_fetched:

Given this, the typology's exact category labels, the land-rent passage, and the explicit Krueger/Tullock critique were NOT read in primary text and are not quoted in this brief.

(b) OBTAINED — Mushtaq H. Khan (2010), 'Political Settlements and the Governance of Growth-Enhancing Institutions,' SOAS working paper (self-archived at eprints.soas.ac.uk/9968/, per the queue). eprints.soas.ac.uk was unreachable for this record too, but the same author-uploaded text is mirrored at thepolicypractice.com/sites/default/files/2023-03/Political_Settlements_and_the_Governance_of_Growth.pdf (a UK development-consultancy site hosting the freely-circulated working paper) and was fetched successfully (HTTP 200, 1.4MB, 61-page working paper plus appendices) and parsed in full with pymupdf; saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/khan-political-settlements-2010.pdf (extracted text: khan-political-settlements-2010.txt). Page numbers below are the paper's own printed page numbers (confirmed against the in-text page-number strings pymupdf extracts on each page), not PDF sheet indices.

(c) NOT PURSUED SEPARATELY — no additional peer-reviewed Khan article was fetched beyond (b); WebSearch surfaced but did not retrieve a JSTOR-hosted piece ('Rival definitions of economic rent...', Taylor & Francis) that looks adjacent but was not opened.

content_summary:
From Khan (2010), 'Political Settlements and the Governance of Growth-Enhancing Institutions' (all quotes verbatim, page numbers as printed on the page):

1. Rents are not uniformly damaging. 'Some of these rents are very damaging in comparison with alternative feasible ways of organizing society. But other rents... may be essential for maintaining stability and preventing a descent into violence' (p. 31), and some 'even in these contexts may be playing a vital role in supporting the development of productive assets and technological capabilities' (p. 31, citing Khan 2000a, 2000b — i.e. the two inaccessible 2000 chapters). This is the paper's clearest statement of a growth-enhancing/growth-reducing (or at least damaging/essential/productive) distinction among rents, though the 2010 paper does not itself use the phrase 'growth-enhancing rents' as a rent-typology label — only 'growth-enhancing institutions.'

2. Implicit qualification of the Krueger/Tullock 'rent-seeking is always wasteful' position (not named in this text — 0 occurrences of 'Krueger' or 'Tullock' in the 140-page extracted text). Discussing South Korea's industrial policy: 'all rent-seeking activities of powerful capitalists are not necessarily damaging from a growth and development perspective. Powerful capitalists can induce ruling coalitions to promote productive sectors even if they are not immediately very productive' (pp. 72-73).

3. Korea comparative evidence. On South Korea's political settlement enabling disciplined industrial policy: 'These characteristics of the South Korean political settlement allowed the implementation of an industrial policy that not only directed significant resources to a growing productive sector, but was also able to enforce discipline and compulsion to ensure high levels of effort in learning' (p. 72) — attributed to the political weakness of Korean capitalists after Japanese rule/occupation, which let the state discipline rent recipients (citing Amsden 1989; Kohli 1994; Khan 2000a). Contrasted with Thaksin-era Thailand (dominant-party capture of monopoly rents for populist redistribution, p. 72) and with South Asia's 1950s-60s pattern of rapid but undisciplined rent-driven accumulation that 'faded as industrial policy to raise productivity growth through resource re-allocation was successfully resisted' (p. 73).

4. Natural-resource rents specifically (land rent is NOT discussed anywhere in this paper — zero occurrences of 'land rent' in the full text; the paper's 'rents' are licenses, protection, subsidies, and resource windfalls, not Ricardian/Georgist land rent). On Tanzania: 'The availability of aid rents and natural resource rents further weakens the incentives of the ruling coalition to develop the politically weak productive sector with proactive policies' (p. 75) — a resource-curse-adjacent mechanism (rents substitute for the political need to cultivate a productive tax base), distinct from the corruption/patronage mechanism the wiki's existing resource-curse coverage emphasizes.

5. 'Learning rents' (Khan's own recurring term in this paper, not defined by that name in the 2000 typology as summarized by third parties): rents deliberately allocated (subsidized credit, protection, licenses) to accelerate technology acquisition, illustrated with India (Maharashtra vs. West Bengal industrial licensing, pp. 130+) and Bangladesh (Multifibre Arrangement quota rents 'fortuitously' building the garment sector's technological base, p. 139) case studies, sourced to Khan (2008) figures reproduced as an appendix.

WebSearch snippets (NOT independently verified against primary text, so not quotable) suggest the 2000 chapters use 'transformation potential' for a state's capacity to convert rent-seeking into learning-linked rents, and distinguish the direction/beneficiary of rent-seeking (input) from whether growth results (outcome) as Khan's answer to why Krueger/Tullock's 'always wasteful' framing fails to explain decades of Asian growth under heavy rent allocation — this characterization should be treated as a lead for a T1 with primary-text access, not as citable content.
existing_wiki_coverage: No existing coverage of Mushtaq Khan anywhere in the corpus digest (no people/mushtaq-khan page; zero hits for 'Khan' as an author in concepts/rent-seeking.md, concepts/economic-rent.md, or concepts/resource-rents.md). concepts/rent-seeking.md (50-line stub-adjacent page) currently frames rent-seeking entirely through Tullock (1967)/Krueger (1974) with no discussion of when/whether rent-seeking or rent allocation can be growth-enhancing — Khan's political-economy qualification would be new to that page, not a duplicate. concepts/economic-rent.md's own 'Rent-Seeking' section is a two-sentence cross-reference to the same page. concepts/resource-rents.md and problems/rent-revenue-breeds-corruption.md cover the resource curse via Colombia (research/martinez-colombia-resource-rents.md, local tax effort/accountability) and via Corruption of Economics' South Africa/Russia/China cases (privatized rent driving corruption) — Khan's Tanzania mechanism (resource/aid rents weakening the ruling coalition's own incentive to build a productive tax base) is a related but distinct causal story worth adding alongside those, not already present. research/schwerhoff-taxation-economic-rents.md has an unrelated 'seven-type rent typology' (regulation/political/investment/natural-monopoly/market-power/inframarginal/scarcity rents) from a different (public-economics, not development-economics) tradition — no overlap in terminology or claims with what was actually read here, so no conflict to reconcile, but a future page drawing on the real Khan typology (once accessible) should be careful not to conflate the two typologies. development-economics/political-settlements framing is otherwise entirely absent from the wiki.
uncertainties: (1) The item T1 most needs to check: this brief could NOT access Khan's core theoretical chapters ('Rents, Efficiency and Growth' and 'Rent-Seeking as Process', 2000) despite exhausting the full access ladder across seven distinct hosts/methods (see what_was_fetched) — the typology (monopoly/natural-resource/Schumpeterian/learning/management rent labels, if that is even Khan's actual terminology), the land-rent-specific passage the task asked for, and the explicit named critique of Krueger and Tullock all remain unverified. Any page text about these must either be deferred until a session with different network access can reach eprints.soas.ac.uk or one of its mirrors, or be sourced to a different, reachable Khan text. (2) The 2010 paper that WAS read is about political settlements and industrial-policy institutions, not land or Georgist rent capture — it mentions 'natural resource rent(s)' only 4 times in 140 pages and 'land rent' zero times; a NEW page built from it should not be framed as if it were Khan's land-rent argument, and should not overstate its relevance to LVT specifically — its real contribution to this wiki is the growth-enhancing/growth-reducing rent-seeking qualification and the resource-curse-adjacent 'rents weaken state incentive to build productive institutions' mechanism. (3) The mirror used (thepolicypractice.com) is not the canonical repository copy; content matches the known abstract/title/version string but was not cross-checked byte-for-byte against eprints.soas.ac.uk. (4) Mushtaq Khan is not yet in sources/audit/people-tiers.json; this brief judges him Tier 1 by the §4c rubric (SOAS professor, large peer-reviewed/highly-cited body of work) but a T1 editor should confirm and add the entry rather than have it default silently.
